jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 3—whether scientific knowledge of the articles of faith can be communicated to a wayfarer—with a reference to Henry of Ghent's Quodlibet VIII.

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e124.summary: First argument that God could give a pure wayfarer certain, express, or scientific knowledge of the articles: any cognition that does not place one outside the state of the wayfarer can be communicated, since all repugnance reduces to contradiction; only intuitive, face-to-face cognition is beatific, and abstractive cognition, however perfect, is less perfect and leaves one desiring intuition.
claims: Whatever does not remove one from the wayfarer's state can be communicated to a wayfarer (objection)
Only intuitive cognition of God is beatific; abstractive cognition is not (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e163.summary: Second argument: what is prior can exist without what is posterior; abstractive cognition, regarding quiddity absolutely, is prior to intuitive cognition, which adds presential existence, so the former can be had without the latter, leaving one a wayfarer.
claims: Abstractive cognition is prior to intuitive cognition and separable from it (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e186.summary: Third argument: whatever the divine essence would cause as a naturally moving object present to the intellect, the divine will can cause without that presence; the essence so present would cause perfect knowledge of itself and all in it, so God can cause such knowledge without presence—and that would be abstractive.
claims: The divine will can supply the causality of any moving object (objection)
God could cause perfect knowledge of his essence without its presence, i.e. abstractively (objection)
concepts: divine will as supplying secondary causes

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e212.summary: Fourth argument: Paul after his rapture remembered the vision of the divine essence (2 Cor 12); this memory was abstractive, so such cognition is possible without intuition. Then the argument to the contrary: abstractive knowledge of God is either as perfect as intuitive (and so equally beatific and incommunicable) or less perfect—but the latter is refuted since God's eternal abstractive knowledge of creatures is not surpassed by his later intuitive knowledge, else God would progress in knowledge.
claims: Paul's memory of his rapture was abstractive knowledge of God (objection)
Abstractive knowledge is not less perfect than intuitive, since God does not progress in knowledge (contrary argument)

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e256.summary: Outlines the response: first present and explain an opinion that a wayfarer can be given perfect, certain, express abstractive (not intuitive) knowledge that God is three and one; then examine its truth.
claims: The opinion to be examined holds that perfect abstractive knowledge of the Trinity can be given to a wayfarer

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e272.summary: Explains the opinion's distinction: intuitive cognition bears immediately on a thing present according to its actual existence; abstractive cognition is any cognition of a thing not so present as immediately known object—including not only abstraction of quiddity from existence but also knowledge that something exists without its presence (the astronomer's eclipse, the philosopher's demonstration that God exists). On this sense, they hold that God could give a wayfarer abstractive quidditative knowledge of himself so perfect as to know with certainty everything intrinsic to God, including the Trinity, since knowing a subject's nature perfectly yields knowledge of its predicates.
claims: Intuitive cognition bears immediately on a present existing thing, abstractive on what is not so present
Abstractive cognition includes knowledge of existence without presence, not only abstraction of quiddity
On the opinion, perfect quidditative abstractive knowledge of God would yield certain knowledge of the Trinity

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e372.summary: Durandus's position: a wayfarer can have abstractive knowledge of God concluded from creatures (which does not reach the Trinity) and express knowledge of the Trinity by faith, but abstractive knowledge as perfect as the opinion holds seems impossible—saving reverence for divine power. First proof: abstractive cognition can never be first but must follow a prior cognition from which it is derived, and no such prior cognition is available to a wayfarer. The major is shown by induction: God knows other things abstractively only by intuiting his essence, angels by intuiting their own essence, and humans and brutes only after sensory intuition.
claims: A wayfarer's abstractive knowledge of God from creatures does not extend to the Trinity
Abstractive cognition always presupposes a prior cognition from which it derives
In God, angels, humans, and brutes, abstractive cognition follows intuitive cognition

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e431.summary: Defends the induction against the reply that it holds only for the common course of nature. If God made interior powers act on external things without prior external sensation, they would have an immediate order to things and their acts would be intuitive, not abstractive; so abstractive cognition necessarily presupposes another. Rational proof: the first cognition must be of actual being (Metaphysics IX), and such cognition, bearing immediately on an existing thing, is intuitive. The minor: no prior cognition can ground such abstraction—not of a creature (shown earlier), nor of God abstractively (infinite regress), nor intuitively, since that is beatific and incommunicable.
claims: Abstractive cognition is necessarily, not just naturally, preceded by another cognition
If interior powers acted without prior sensation, their acts would be intuitive
The first cognition is of actual being and is intuitive
No prior cognition available to a wayfarer could ground perfect abstractive knowledge of God

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e562.summary: Notes the objection that, though not to one who was never a comprehensor, such abstractive knowledge could be given after a rapture to intuitive vision, as with Paul; the matter is deferred to the reply to the fourth argument.
claims: The Pauline-rapture objection is deferred to the replies

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e580.summary: Second proof of the main conclusion: such knowledge would require the divine essence to be present either immediately—making the cognition intuitive and beatific—or through something else, either a known medium (but nothing created can lead to express knowledge of the Trinity) or a mere ratio cognoscendi like a species. But a species presenting a really present thing yields intuitive cognition, and the divine essence is really present to every power and thing; so a species presenting it would yield intuitive cognition.
claims: Immediate presence of the divine essence would make the cognition intuitive
No created known medium leads to express knowledge of the Trinity
A species presenting a really present object yields intuitive, not abstractive, cognition
The divine essence is really present to every cognitive power

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e630.summary: Completes the argument: a species presenting the divine essence to a capable power would produce intuitive cognition, which is how some explain the species in beatific vision. Durandus himself denies that any species could represent the divine essence for intuitive or abstractive knowledge, deferring to Book IV.
claims: Some posit a species in beatific vision
No species can represent the divine essence

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e646.summary: Raises an objection to the second proof: an object need not be present by existence, known medium, or species, since only the act of cognition makes the object present 'as known'; real presence is required only when the object causes the cognition, and God can do by himself what he does through an object, so he could cause knowledge of something not present in any way.
claims: Objection: only the cognitive act makes an object present as known
Objection: God could cause cognition of an object without any presence of it

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e685.summary: Replies that this seems absurd at first sight, since it would let God make the eye see a nonexistent color, the ear hear a nonexistent sound, and so with all senses—which many think impossible.
claims: If no presence of the object were required, the senses could perceive nonexistent objects, which seems impossible

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e709.summary: Further reply: created cognition requires the presence of its object more than uncreated cognition, since more perfect cognition requires less; yet divine cognition requires its objects to be present in reality or in their representative—God's essence directly, creatures eternally in the essence representing them. Hence all created cognition requires its object's real presence or representative. The prior argument stands, and no wayfarer can by any power have abstractive knowledge of God sufficient to know with certainty that God is three.
claims: More perfect cognition requires fewer conditions than less perfect cognition
Even divine cognition requires its objects present in reality or in a representative
No wayfarer, by any power, can have abstractive knowledge of God sufficient to know the Trinity

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e762.summary: Reply to the first argument, identifying a twofold defect. First, communicable perfection must be possible in itself; the abstractive cognition posited is possible for no knower—not God (it is imperfect), not the blessed as blessed (their cognition is intuitive), and not the wayfarer (as shown). Second, 'human wayfarer' combines overlapping notions, so the major must require compatibility with being human and with being a wayfarer; the argument proves only the latter. Thus it is defective in three ways.
claims: Only what is possible in itself can be communicated
The posited abstractive cognition is possible for no knower
What is repugnant to a human wayfarer qua human need not be repugnant qua wayfarer

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e847.summary: Reply to the second argument by denying the minor: intuitive cognition is prior to abstractive, as external sensation shows, so intuitive can exist without abstractive and not conversely. Abstractive cognition is not related to intuitive by addition; and the argument from the order of objects fails both generally (accidents are posterior to substance yet known first) and in God, whose existence is not added to his quiddity.
claims: Intuitive cognition is prior to abstractive
Priority among objects does not determine priority among cognitions
In God existence and quiddity are identical
concepts: order of knowing vs. order of being
identity of essence and existence in God

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e895.summary: Reply to the third argument: it works against the opponents, since the divine essence present as a naturally moving object would cause perfect intuitive, not abstractive, knowledge; so what the divine will could supply would be intuitive cognition.
claims: The divine essence present as moving object would cause intuitive knowledge, so God's supplying it would yield intuition, not abstraction

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e930.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: Paul's memory after the rapture was not express cognition of the divine essence or of the beatific vision, but a confused recollection of having seen God, like Nebuchadnezzar's memory of a great dream (Daniel 2). Memory works through an impression representing its object as a known medium, and nothing created can represent the divine essence expressly and quidditatively.
claims: Paul retained only a confused memory of having seen God
Memory works through an impression representing its object as a medium
Nothing created can represent the divine essence expressly and quidditatively

jsnvu6-d1e110-d1e965.summary: Reply to the contrary argument: though its conclusion agrees, it wrongly assumes that abstractive cognition of the same power and object is as perfect as intuitive, and that God had abstractive knowledge of creatures before having intuitive knowledge. God has a single, invariant cognition of all things, representing creatures as secondary objects through his essence whether they exist or not, so his knowledge is no more abstractive or intuitive at one time than another—unlike ours.
claims: Abstractive cognition is not as perfect as intuitive cognition of the same object
God has a single, uniformly perfect cognition of creatures
The intuitive/abstractive distinction does not apply to God as it does to us

jsnvu6-d1e110.summary: Question 3 asks whether scientific (certain and express) knowledge of the articles could be communicated to a wayfarer by divine power. Durandus reports an opinion that God could give a pure wayfarer abstractive—not intuitive—knowledge of himself so perfect as to know the Trinity with certainty, abstractive cognition being any knowledge of a thing not present as immediately known object. He denies this possibility, while reserving divine power. First, abstractive cognition always presupposes a prior cognition, ultimately an intuitive cognition of actual being; this holds necessarily, not just naturally, and the only prior cognition that could ground knowledge of the Trinity is the beatific intuition itself. Second, the divine essence could be presented only immediately or through a species, either of which would make the cognition intuitive, since the essence is really present everywhere; the objection that cognition needs no presence of its object is rejected, as even divine knowledge requires its objects present in reality or in a representative. In the replies he argues that such a cognition is possible for no knower, that intuitive cognition is prior to abstractive, that Paul retained only a confused memory of his vision, and that God's single cognition is neither more abstractive nor more intuitive over time.
claims: A wayfarer cannot, by any power, have abstractive knowledge of God perfect enough to know the Trinity with certainty
Abstractive cognition necessarily presupposes a prior, ultimately intuitive, cognition
Any presentation of the divine essence, immediate or through a species, would make the cognition intuitive and beatific
Cognition requires its object's presence in reality or in a representative
Paul retained only a confused memory of his rapture
